title: Bilateral Strategic Partnerships as Architecture of International Order: Enabling Conditions, Dimensional Balance, and Resilience in Four Partnership Models, 2015–2025
content: Bilateral strategic partnerships (BSPs) have become a pivotal instrument of interstate cooperation, yet the concept remains undertheorized and systematic cross-case analysis of partnership structure and resilience is scarce. This study constructs a four-axis analytical framework distinguishing BSPs from cognate forms of cooperation and applies it, through reflexive thematic analysis and structured focused comparison, to four paradigmatic models—Franco-German, U.S.–Japan, Sino-Russian, and Saudi–U.S.—drawing on treaty texts, joint communiqués, official policy documents, institutional statistics, and peer-reviewed scholarship from 2015 to 2025. Three findings emerge. Partnership durability rests on four interdependent enabling conditions, of which institutional architecture alone discriminates among outcomes and alone compensates for weakness elsewhere in the system. Dimensional balance is analytically distinct from dimensional depth, and balanced partnerships absorb shocks that skewed partnerships do not. Typological placement is dynamic rather than fixed: the Saudi–U.S. case demonstrates how a partnership anchored historically in a single functional domain can be deliberately broadened into a multidimensional framework through a national transformation strategy, exercising strategic agency over the terms of its most consequential external relationship. The study concludes that BSPs function not merely as bilateral instruments but as constitutive building blocks of a polycentric international order, while cautioning against the inflationary deployment of the partnership label.
